content.value: Since I moved to Seattle five years ago, I’ve become a big WNBA fan. (Let’s go, Storm.) I’ve also become fixated on a question. Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?
fox-iran-wnba.png | Fox News homepage navigation listing its Hot Topics: War With Iran, then WNBA Controversy
This question dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News.

The first clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, my Google Chrome app recommended more WNBA news. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News.
Wait, what?
It wasn’t just one article, either. I saw dozens of Fox News takes on women’s basketball, often with a clear political bias, and an implicitly racist and homophobic framing.
Caitlin Clark, Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese

Headline after headline pitted the league’s most famous straight white star, Caitlin Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.
So, data nerd that I am, I started collecting headlines. How does Fox News cover the WNBA compared to everybody else?

steps.text: If all outlets talked about Caitin Clark equally, she’d be here in the middle.
But Fox News discusses Caitlin Clark significantly more than other outlets.

content.value: Why the outsized focus on Carrington, Cloud, and Griner? It’s political.
DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner

Carrington has publicly criticized Clark for various reasons, including for not being vocal enough in denouncing her bigoted fans. She has also fouled Clark and Cunningham, darlings of Fox News. And she doesn’t like Trump [[Jan 2025 | WNBA star ==DiJonai Carrington== flaunts explicit message on pre-game outfit directed at President Trump]].

Similarly, Cloud’s outspoken activism—for Black Lives Matter, for Gaza—has been a focal point [[WNBA player ==Natasha Cloud== calls out Israel on Oct 7 while blaming Republicans for government shutdown]]. And Griner was the subject of consistent conversation when she was imprisoned in Russia in 2022, [[==Brittney Griner== is coming home. Will she stand for the anthem now that she's back in the USA?]] though she is often criticized for her progressive views, too.
It’s not just online coverage. I knew the WNBA was being talked about on Fox News TV programs, too.

At a holiday gathering, I was chatting with an older conservative family member, who, out of the blue, started name-dropping WNBA players—saying praiseworthy things about Clark and suspect things about other Black players.
This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

steps.text: Sure enough, Fox talks more about Clark ((Caitlin Clark| face)) and Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham| face)) on TV, too.
This is cable news coverage of the WNBA, via their chyrons—you know, those headlines that appear at the bottom of your screen.
Fox News talks incessantly about fouls against Clark.
They also talk way more about trans women in sports.
Especially recently.
Search any term.

content.value: In summer 2026, the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream. In July, Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham|face)), the Fever’s shooting guard, made openly anti-trans remarks, which inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her—including Vice President J.D. Vance and J.K. Rowling.
vance-cunningham-fox.png | Fox News segment showing Vice President J.D. Vance praising Sophie Cunningham | Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Even Fox News political pundits are confused and exhausted by the WNBA coverage. As Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”
https://www.youtube.com/shorts/k1aa6ip2HA4
How did professional women’s basketball—a league that, for decades, most people didn’t watch or care anything about—transform into a mainstream political lightning rod?
It didn’t happen overnight. And the media, especially conservative media, played a role.
So let’s dive into how Fox News framed the WNBA as a hot-button culture war issue—one that was primed, at the right moment, to explode.
The Data

What matters is not only how often certain media outlets discuss the WNBA, or how they talk about some WNBA players versus others. It’s how these issues and players are actually discussed, and who they are paired with or against.

To explore this in depth, I collected any Fox News article that mentioned the WNBA or its players over the past six years. This includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox (“the antidote to the mainstream sports media that often serves an elite, left-leaning minority”).

value.caption: Every article has a headline; full text where the outlet allows it. The Athletic is paywalled, so it is headlines only. Counts run through Aug 2026.

content.value: As a comparison, I collected articles from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

Additionally, I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN—drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool previous analysis by Charlie Smart.
Let’s look at the broad timeline. For most of its history, Fox News barely covered the WNBA. They talked about the NBA much more.

value.caption: Mentions of Caitlin Clark in Fox WNBA articles

content.value: But you can see that coverage clearly surges in the “Caitlin Clark era”—that is, after Clark was drafted into the league in April 2024.
Fox News’s coverage of the WNBA, however, has always been political. One way they’ve achieved this: a reliable cast of characters.
The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe

Fox News often speaks the most loudly through the individuals they platform, using them as mouthpieces. What’s more, they pit players against each other in ways that amplify divisive political narratives.

content.value: The WNBA’s Political Activism
When covering the WNBA recently, Fox News insists that women’s basketball should have nothing to do with race, gender, or politics.
Here’s the irony: when discussing the WNBA, Fox News talks about race, gender, and politics more than any other outlet.

value.title: WNBA Articles that Mention Race or BLM Protest
value.caption: Words include: racism, racist, racial, white privilege, “Black/white” + women/players/athletes/stars/community, social justice, Black Lives Matter, BLM, anthem, protest, kneel, boycott, police shooting, election, indictment.

content.value: Fox News has been obsessed with dispelling the identity-related dimension of this narrative. At the same time, Fox News has played up Clark’s treatment in the league, specifically hard fouls committed against her, often in implicitly racialized terms that malign the Black and/or queer players who committed the fouls.
In 2020, WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of the Black Lives Matter movement.

wnba-blm-2020.jpg | Minnesota Lynx players standing with linked arms, wearing “Say Her Name” shirts | Minnesota Lynx players wear “Say Her Name” shirts and lock arms during a moment of silence in honor of Breonna Taylor before a game in July 2020. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP

They walked off the court during the national anthem, wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television, and successfully campaigned to unseat a team owner who sat in the U.S. Senate, Kelly Loeffler, after she opposed players’ activism.
The WNBA’s engagement with protest and racial justice conversations was frequently covered by Fox, and often framed in implicitly disapproving terms.
the protests | July 2020 | green | WNBA players ==walk off court during national anthem== ahead of season opener
the protests | July 2020 | green | Sen. Kelly Loeffler, co-owner of Atlanta Dream, ==objects to WNBA's social justice plans==
the protests | July 2020 | green | WNBA players call on league to ==stop playing national anthem== before games
the protests | August 2020 | green | WNBA team wears shirts with ==Jacob Blake's name==, league postpones games following Kenosha shooting
Increasingly, they also spotlighted the league’s LGBTQ+ players and related issues, including trans rights and trans women’s participation in sports.

value.title: WNBA Articles that Mention LGBTQ+ Topics
value.caption: Share of each outlet's WNBA articles, by year. Words counted: LGBT/LGBTQ, lesbian, gay, queer, sexual orientation, same-sex, Athlete Ally, Pride Night, Pride Month, bisexual, nonbinary.

content.value: In spring 2023, Megan Rapinoe and Sue Bird signed a letter opposing a bill restricting transgender athletes, and Brittney Griner backed trans participation in sports.
the letter | April 2023 | teal | Megan Rapinoe, Sue Bird among athletes who sign letter ==opposing Protection of Girls and Women in Sports Act==
griner speaks | April 2023 | teal | Brittney Griner ==backs transgender participation in sports==: ‘A crime’ to ‘separate someone for any reason’

In response, Fox News platformed swimmer and anti-trans advocate Riley Gaines, who called Griner’s remarks “heartbreaking,” as well as former NBA player Enes Kanter, who suggested that if trans women were allowed to join the WNBA, he would, too. This is a hateful stunt that he has revived in 2026.
the response | April 2023 | teal | Riley Gaines calls Brittney Griner's remarks on transgender athlete participation ==‘heartbreaking’==
the escalation | August 2023 | teal | Enes Freedom on trans athletes in women's sports: ==‘Should I put on a wig ... and start dominating the WNBA?’==
Then, in 2024, Caitlin Clark arrived. And the culture war WNBA conversation heated up even more.
Enter Caitlin Clark

Caitlin Clark, the three-point phenom from Iowa, was drafted #1 by the Indiana Fever in 2024. Her popularity has drawn millions of new viewers and fans to the league. But it has also launched the WNBA into a culture war/identity politics debate that often has little to do with the league itself.

clark-fever-spurlock.jpg | Caitlin Clark, seen from behind in her white Indiana Fever number 22 jersey, releases a jump shot toward the basket. | Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Many commentators have noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal. It is undeniable that Clark has drawn in a whiter, more conservative, and more mainstream audience than the WNBA—a historically Black and queer league—has had in the past.

Fox News has been obsessed with dispelling the identity-related dimension of this narrative. At the same time, Fox News has played up Clark’s treatment in the league, specifically hard fouls committed against her, often in implicitly racialized terms that malign the Black and/or queer players who committed the fouls.

steps.text: Case in point: Fox News has consistently discussed “hard” fouls against Caitlin Clark more than other outlets.

steps.words: race, racism, racist, privilege, black, white
steps.text: They also invoked race and racism more than other outlets, as well as culture war buzzwords like “privilege.”

This is especially true because trolls “will just use this controversy to denigrate the rest of the WNBA. “No amount of good PR,” she warns, “is going to stop clickbait or the right’s obsession with criticizing the WNBA.”

content.value: Who Gets Framed How?
Trans Women in Sports

Fox News consistently fanned the flames of the WNBA culture war. They denied that race, sexuality, or gender were relevant considerations in the league, yet foregrounded them more than any other outlet.

The implicit misogyny, and suspicion of “social justice” and queer communities, laid the groundwork for the right-wing, anti-trans movement to rise up and seize the WNBA as a central issue—even though no trans women currently even play in the league.

value.title: Fox WNBA articles about trans athletes
value.caption: Fox WNBA articles per month that mention trans athletes or eligibility in women’s sports. Source: Fox News.

steps.text: Through 2025, Fox planted the seed for controversy around trans issues and the WNBA, discussing it periodically but consistently.
Then, in 2026, it exploded.
And as a share of everything Fox writes about the WNBA, trans coverage went from a sliver to the majority: in August 2026, nearly two out of every three Fox WNBA articles mention trans athletes.

value.title: Anti-trans rhetoric
value.caption: Share of Fox WNBA articles each month containing trans language (“trans,” “transgender,” or “biological males”) or “protect” — as in “protecting women’s sports” — smoothed with a 5-month window.

content.value: Among the TV networks, Fox News talks about trans issues way more than the others.

As Jesse Watters recently said on air, “Why are we covering the WNBA?” Or, more pointedly, “This is something I don’t care about.” Watters said the quiet part out loud. Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. Right-wing pundits and politicians are using the WNBA to push their own agenda.

Sports are political. They have always been political. Throughout American history, athletes have been able to use their platform to advocate for justice. Players in the WNBA are a great example. But we should be wary of how narratives about the WNBA are being framed by the right-wing media and outside parties who have little to no actual investment in the league.

When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt. It was completely different from every other (men’s) professional sporting event I had ever been to. The version of the WNBA presented by Fox News is not recognizable to me. We need to recognize this framing—and push back against it—lest we all get played.
Data and Methods
I collected WNBA articles from Fox News, ESPN, Yahoo Sports, Just Women’s Sports, The Athletic, CBS Sports, and USA Today.
The chyrons come from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye project.
The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).
You can find data and code on GitHub.
